claims.text: The starting material is a conventional W–Cu metal-matrix composite made by standard processing routes.
An ultrathin carbide or graphene coating can be introduced at the W–Cu interface using a technique such as atomic layer deposition.
The interfacial coating will reduce thermal boundary resistance between W and Cu.
Reducing W–Cu interfacial thermal resistance will increase the composite's overall thermal conductivity.
The coating will increase thermal conductivity without degrading mechanical durability.
The coating will increase thermal conductivity without degrading irradiation resistance.
The coating acts as a tailored interphase that enhances adhesion between W and Cu.
The tailored interphase minimizes phonon scattering at the W–Cu interface.
Lower thermal boundary resistance permits more effective phonon transfer between the phases.
Lower thermal boundary resistance permits more effective electron transfer between the phases.
A robust interfacial coating will preserve interface integrity during mechanical loading.
A robust interfacial coating will preserve interface integrity during irradiation and thereby resist radiation-induced damage.
Reactor-relevant fusion applications involve elevated-temperature and irradiation exposure.
The coated W–Cu composite will have higher thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable uncoated W–Cu composite.
The coated composite will retain mechanical strength comparable to the uncoated control.
The coated composite will retain irradiation resistance comparable to the uncoated control.
The predicted benefit depends on the interfacial layer being uniformly ultrathin, chemically stable, and well bonded to both phases.
